$$

problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}-{w}^{2} \\ w{e}^{u} \\ u-v\end{bmatrix}.
$$
worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-{w}^{2},\,y(u,v,w)=w{e}^{u},\,z(u,v,w)=u-v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-2w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =w{e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & ={e}^{u} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 & -2w \\ w{e}^{u} & 0 & {e}^{u} \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2u\begin{vmatrix}0 & {e}^{u} \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}-2w\begin{vmatrix}w{e}^{u} & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2u(0+{e}^{u})-2w(-w{e}^{u}-0) \\  & =2u{e}^{u}+2{w}^{2}{e}^{u} \\  & =2{e}^{u}({w}^{2}+u).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2{e}^{u}({w}^{2}+u) & =0 \\ {w}^{2}+u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation ${w}^{2}+u=0$ defines the parabolic cylinder $u=-{w}^{2}.$

problem:
Let $C$ be the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x+y=1,$ $x=0,$ and $y=0.$ Given that the curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and $\text{curl}\,F=⟨-2z,\,0,\,0⟩,$ the circulation of $F$ along $C$ can be written as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr=
$$
worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-2z,\,0,\,0⟩{|}_{z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨-2(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨\underbrace{2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20}_{P},\,\underbrace{0}_{Q},\,\underbrace{0}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20)\cdot (-2x)-0\cdot (-2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/c1/c181e209cca01a1d6e372caa7f7810a5fa4aa9f177595bd92f937a7cba8b8a75.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\,4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
![](images/0c/0c46972a3968d7110cb08d4b16bfff9267e49b102cf005cdbb21a3630d15c49d.png)

Consider the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal radius $7$ and vertical radius $2,$ as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$  traverse the ellipse once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(7,0)?$
worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=b\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the ellipse is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(a,0).$

In our case, $a=7$ and $b=2.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the ellipse are

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

problem:
![](images/14/14d1fc5a92c28cc7f84c1ec23929701f1aca67b1a15d6113fa83f1428354fc11.png)

Consider the ellipse centered at $(3,-1)$ with horizontal radius $2$ and vertical radius $3,$ as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$  traverse the ellipse once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(5,-1)?$
worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the point $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +h,\,y=b\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +k,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the ellipse is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(h+a,k).$

In our case, the ellipse is centered at the point $(3,-1),$ $a=2$ and $b=3.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the ellipse are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

problem: Which of the following is *not* a simply connected region?

problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y?$
worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y) \\  & =2x \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =2x\,i-j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-2,1),$ $(0,2),$ and $(2,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,1) & =2\cdot (-2)\,i-j=-4\,i-j \\ ∇f(0,2) & =2\cdot (0)\,i-j=-\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =2\cdot 2\,i-j=4\,i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

problem:
Let $F(x,y,z)={y}^{2}\,i-{x}^{2}\,j+5\,k$ and let $C$ be a path in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?
$$
worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y+R(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x-{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y+5\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2x+y}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(0,1),$ $(1,0),$ $(-1,3),$ and $(0,2).$
worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2x+y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=2x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(0,1) & =(0+1,2(0)+1) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(1+0,2(1)+0) \\  & =(1,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(-1,3) & =(-1+3,2(-1)+3) \\  & =(2,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(0,2) & =(0+2,2(0)+2) \\  & =(2,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 2}
$$

![](images/3a/3a831bbc56c0ce5e749fcf45bd65825f297d7732158b8f9e371f2178e61b92c0.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-1
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2x+y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{{u}^{2}}{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{{u}^{2}}{v}\,|-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{{u}^{2}}{v}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{u}^{2}}{v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[\operatorname{ln}⁡v]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le 2y+z\le 1,\,1\le y-2z\le 4}.
$$
worked_solution:
Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V={∭}_{R}\text{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le 2y+z\le 1,\,1\le y-2z\le 4,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x,\,v=2y+z,\,w=y-2z.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 1,\,1\le w\le 4}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}dV & ={∭}_{Δ}1\cdot |-\frac{1}{5}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{5}\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}du\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}dv\cdot {\int }_{1}^{4}dw \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[u]_{0}^{1}\cdot [v]_{-1}^{1}\cdot [w]_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (1-(-1))\cdot (4-1) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-1,1)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}v{e}^{u} \\ u{e}^{v}\end{bmatrix}?
$$
worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot \underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}v{e}^{u} & {e}^{u} \\ {e}^{v} & u{e}^{v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =v{e}^{u}\cdot u{e}^{v}-{e}^{v}\cdot {e}^{u} \\  & =uv{e}^{u+v}-{e}^{u+v} \\  & =(uv-1){e}^{u+v} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-1,1)} & =(uv-1){e}^{u+v}\,{|}_{u=-1\,v=1} \\  & =(-1\cdot 1-1){e}^{-1+1} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-2|\cdot \delta A \\  & =2\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$
